reply.title: Squashing with the Logistic Curve
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or population growth, raw numbers can range from negative infinity to positive infinity. Yet we often need an answer that stays strictly between zero and one. Pierre François Verhulst faced this problem when studying population limits and used a special S-shaped curve to bend unlimited inputs into a bounded range.

This curve maps any input $x$ smoothly between zero and one. Its steepness $k$ controls how abruptly the transition happens, while the midpoint $x_0$ shifts where the transition centers. At the center, the output is exactly one half and the slope reaches its maximum value.

By adjusting the steepness and midpoint, we see how the S-shaped logistic function squashes wide inputs into a clean proportion. The tangent line at the marker reveals how fast the output changes for a given input, showing the power of nonlinear squashing.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic curve maps any input to a bounded range between zero and one. Adjust the steepness and midpoint to see the S-shaped transition change.
reply.instructions: Adjust the sliders to change the steepness and midpoint of the curve. Observe how the output and tangent slope update at the marker.
